relationships.relationship: Ratio falls while nominal debt rises

passages.text: The figure is INSEE's Maastricht debt: what central government, local authorities and social security owe, at face value. Two steps account for most of the rise. Debt rose 18.6 points of GDP from end-2007 to end-2009, and 16.7 points in 2020. Neither step was reversed. After the first, the ratio kept climbing until 2017. After the second, it eased to 109.5% at end-2023, then rose again. That dip came from an economy growing faster than the debt, not from repayment: the debt in euros kept rising. It now stands at €3.6 trillion.

relationships.relationship: Interest relief reverses and adds fiscal pressure

passages.text: That offset is now reversing. Interest cost 3.6% of GDP in 1996 and 1.3% in 2020; by 2025 it was back to 2.2%. INSEE [attributes the 2025 increase](https://www.insee.fr/fr/statistiques/8997691) to the larger stock of debt and the rise in interest rates since 2022. The same report shows the deficit narrowing from 5.8% in 2024, mainly through new revenue measures, while spending growth slowed with inflation. Many social benefits, pensions among them, are indexed to past inflation.

The data does not say why old-age and health spending grew; ageing, indexation and policy choices each need their own evidence. What it does show is the gap. France raises more than its neighbours, spends more still, and has run a deficit every year for three decades. With interest costs rising again, falling interest no longer makes room for the rest of the budget.

The deficit is the yearly gap between what they spend and what they collect. Each deficit adds to the debt. The ratio falls only when the economy's cash value grows faster than the debt.

France has spent more than it collected in every year since at least 1995, where the series starts. The smallest gap was 1.3% of GDP, in 2000. Leave interest aside and France last ran a surplus in 2001, at 1.7% of GDP. It has run a deficit before interest every year since.

There was a post-pandemic decline in the debt ratio because nominal GDP outgrew debt, but the decline did not reverse the whole jump and has now reversed. The present gap remains substantial before paying interest, while rising interest adds a further burden. France already collects more relative to GDP than the displayed neighbours, and its unusually high spending exceeds that income. Spending composition has shifted toward pensions and health without a comparable long-term rise in its total GDP share. This is an account of persistent fiscal pressure rather than evidence for an immediate market or political crisis.

relationships.relationship: Revenue adequacy inferred from ranking

passages.text: France collects more than its neighbours: 52.1% of GDP in 2025, against 48.1% in Italy, 47.9% in Germany and 42.9% in Spain. It spends more still, 57.2%. Its deficit of 5.1% is the largest of the group. France had the highest revenue and the highest spending of the four countries in every year of the series.

Deficits alone are not unusual. Italy, and the EU as a whole, also ran one every year. The difference is the balance before interest: −2.9% of GDP in France, +0.8% in Italy, which pays more interest. The dataset has no debt figures for the other countries.

record.overall_understanding: The story explains the accumulation of French public debt as a persistent annual financing gap, punctuated by much larger gaps around major shocks. There was a post-pandemic decline in the debt ratio because nominal GDP outgrew debt, but the decline did not reverse the whole jump and has now reversed. The present gap remains substantial before paying interest, while rising interest adds a further burden. France already collects more relative to GDP than the displayed neighbours, and its unusually high spending exceeds that income. Spending composition has shifted toward pensions and health without a comparable long-term rise in its total GDP share. This is an account of persistent fiscal pressure rather than evidence for an immediate market or political crisis.
what_prose_adds_or_changes: It explicitly distinguishes accumulated debt, annual deficits, and the GDP denominator, helping connect why the ratio can fall despite annual deficits.
It identifies the coverage of Maastricht debt as central government, local authorities and social security funds, valued at face value.
It adds the claim that France had the highest spending and revenue of the four countries in every year, not merely in the displayed 2025 snapshot.
It adds that Italy and the EU also ran deficits every year, which makes continuous deficits less specifically French than chart 2 alone might suggest.
It attributes rising interest to both a larger debt stock and rates rising since 2022, citing INSEE; that causal account is new to the prose.
It explicitly says revenue rose too and the gap remained open rather than continuously widening. The spending composition chart alone did not tell me this.

It expressly limits the answer to the commission: the packet cannot explain why crisis is the term used now without yields, ratings or parliamentary events. This matches my earlier unresolved distinction.

The production note supplies provenance, dates and conventions, including EUR67bn under the plotted Eurostat measure versus EUR64.7bn under an INSEE convention. I have not followed or verified those sources.
relationships_between_findings: The annual deficits provide a flow counterpart to the rising debt stock; nominal GDP growth can nevertheless make their ratio fall.
Large deficit years coincide with the conspicuous upward debt steps, while primary deficits persist outside those shock years.

The comparison with Italy separates the burden of servicing past borrowing from the gap in the current budget before interest: Italy has a primary surplus in the snapshot despite a total deficit, whereas France does not.
High revenue and still higher spending coexist. The relative ranking does not by itself demonstrate whether revenue is adequate for the spending commitments.
Higher pension and health shares are partly offset by smaller shares elsewhere, so the categories that grew cannot simply be identified as the cause of the overall deficit.
The interest bill is rising recently but is smaller as a GDP share than in the late 1990s, so the current debt problem cannot be reduced to unprecedented interest costs.
support_and_uncertainty: Most numerical claims directly match the charts. The multiple-year international rankings, yearly Italian/EU deficits and revenue trajectory are additional claims requiring the unreleased underlying data.

quoted_passages.text: **On 20 April 2020 the spot price of WTI crude was −$36.98 a barrel. Brent was $17.36.**
The price of oil did not go below zero. One price did: West Texas Intermediate (WTI), delivered at Cushing, Oklahoma, for one trading day. Where and for how long are the clues to why.

H1.specific_reader_payoff: Distinguish an isolated WTI negative daily event from a shared oil-price slump and positive aggregates; this narrows the event that the commissioned why must explain.

frozen_spontaneous_evidence.record: The pandemic depressed oil demand and both benchmarks. According to the attributed EIA explanation, constrained storage at inland Cushing collided with the approaching May futures contract expiration: holders unable to receive oil needed to sell, while few buyers could accommodate barrels. That produced the extraordinary one-day WTI negative price. The broad slump persisted, but the negative observation and huge Brent–WTI gap were brief.

prose_evidence.text: **On 20 April 2020 the spot price of WTI crude was −$36.98 a barrel. Brent was $17.36.**

The slump was shared. Between 6 January, the highest price of 2020 for both, and Friday 17 April, WTI fell from $63.27 to $18.31 and Brent from $70.25 to $19.75: drops of 71% and 72%. Through March and early April the two moved together, with WTI sometimes the higher of the two.
The fall below zero was not shared. On Monday 20 April WTI went to −$36.98 while Brent stayed at $17.36, $54.34 higher.

It was also brief. WTI was back to $8.91 the next day. Its average for the week ending 24 April was $3.32, and for April as a whole $16.55. Neither average went below zero. By 29 May WTI was at $35.57.

passages.text: The prices show what happened, where and for how long. They do not show why. EIA's [explanation](https://www.eia.gov/todayinenergy/detail.php?id=43495) is this. Pandemic restrictions cut demand for oil sharply, and crude storage at Cushing, the delivery point for the main US WTI futures contract, was filling up. The May 2020 contract expired on 21 April. Holders who could not take delivery of physical barrels at Cushing had to sell, and with tank space short, few buyers could take the oil. So sellers paid buyers to take it.

This data does not test that account, and it cannot rule out other contributors. But the record has the shape the account describes: one inland price, one day, the day before a contract expired, while the seaborne benchmark stayed positive.

The explanation comes from the Commodity Futures Trading Commission's staff review of that day's trading ([interim staff report, November 2020](https://www.cftc.gov/media/5296/InterimStaffReportNYMEX_WTICrude/download)). COVID-19 lockdowns had cut demand for fuel. The May WTI futures contract expired on 21 April, and it is settled by physical delivery of oil at Cushing, where storage was largely full or already committed. Traders holding contracts they could not take delivery of had to sell, and on 20 April buyers had to be paid to take them. Brent futures, by contrast, are settled in cash against an index, not by delivery ([ICE contract specification](https://www.ice.com/products/219/Brent-Crude-Futures)).

The prices are consistent with that account: one benchmark negative, on the day before its contract expired, and positive again the next day. They do not test it. This dataset has no storage, futures-position or demand series.

Brent did not escape. On 21 April, the day after WTI's negative price, Brent fell to $9.12, two cents above its lowest daily price on record, $9.10 in December 1998. Nor was Brent always the dearer crude that spring: on 31 March it was $14.85, against WTI's $20.51. Both markets were at lows not seen since the late 1990s. Only WTI crossed zero, and only on the day before its delivery deadline.

passages.text: The prices show *that* one price went negative, not *why*. The explanation comes from the U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC), whose staff examined the day in an [interim report](https://www.cftc.gov/media/5296/InterimStaffReportNYMEX_WTICrude/download) in November 2020.

The May WTI futures contract expired on 21 April, and it is settled by delivering physical oil at Cushing. Anyone still holding a contract had to take barrels there, and storage at Cushing was scarce. On 20 April, the day before expiry, holders with nowhere to put the oil sold at any price, even below zero. The Cushing spot price went negative the same day.

That account explains why the price that fell was WTI's, and why it fell on that day. The data does not say why Brent stayed positive. The plain difference is where each is priced, a landlocked tank farm against cargoes at sea, but this dataset cannot test it.

passages.text: The data shows what happened, not why. The explanation comes from the EIA, which put the fall down to ["low liquidity and limited available storage"](https://www.eia.gov/todayinenergy/detail.php?id=43495). The May 2020 WTI futures contract expired on 21 April. It is settled by physical delivery of oil at Cushing. Storage there was filling up while demand collapsed under COVID-19 lockdowns ([IEA, *Oil Market Report*, April 2020](https://www.iea.org/reports/oil-market-report-april-2020)). Holders of expiring contracts who could not take delivery had to pay someone else to take the contracts off their hands.

Brent futures work differently. They are settled in cash against an index ([ICE, *Brent Crude Futures*](https://www.ice.com/products/219/Brent-Crude-Futures)), so an expiring Brent contract does not oblige anyone to take barrels.

This dataset cannot test that explanation, but it fits it. The inland, physically delivered benchmark went negative and the waterborne one did not. By the next trading day the price was positive again.

Crisis-year jumps in 2009 and 2020 were never fully reversed, and borrowing continued between them. France collects more revenue than the EU average but spends even more above that average, particularly on cash benefits and public employees. Rising interest bills now add pressure without yet reaching historically exceptional GDP shares.
